comparator.name: Law
comparator.sourceNotes: Leiden began a cohort-by-cohort revision of the Law bachelor in 2025–2026. The transition guide states that only the new first year was introduced for that cohort, while later years continued under the outgoing structure. For 2026–2027 the revised programme is still being phased in: current sources establish the 180-EC degree, the 150-EC compulsory/30-EC free-choice architecture, its Dutch-law learning outcomes and the published current-year course offer, but they do not provide a complete course-level three-year pathway for a student entering in 2026 without combining revised-cohort and outgoing-cohort curricula. The aggregate components below retain only the credit structure directly supported by the regulations.

components.name: Compulsory Law curriculum
components.note: The regulations define 150 EC of compulsory study, including Dutch private, criminal, constitutional and administrative law, international and European law, foundations, skills and the bachelor thesis; the complete revised course-level sequence is not yet published for one current-entry cohort.

components.name: Approved free-choice space
components.note: The regulations define 30 EC of approved free-choice study, including eligible Leiden, Delft, Erasmus or other approved university study.

exception.reason: The Law bachelor is being introduced cohort by cohort. Current official sources support the degree's 180-EC architecture and the revised curriculum published so far, but the complete three-year course-level sequence for a 2026 entrant is not yet available. Combining revised first- and second-year material with the outgoing third-year curriculum would create an unconfirmed pathway, so a fair normal comparison cannot yet be certified.
exception.curriculumContext: The supported structure is 150 EC of compulsory legal study plus 30 EC of approved free-choice space. The compulsory programme is centred on Dutch positive law—private law and civil procedure, criminal law and criminal procedure, constitutional and administrative law and procedure—together with international and European law, legal history and philosophy, research methodology, legal writing and oral argumentation, and a bachelor thesis. The remaining problem is not the degree total or field identity but the absence of one complete current-entry course sequence during the staged redesign. Revisit when Leiden publishes the revised third year.
